chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammad, from Hanan ibn Sudeyr, from his father, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, charity repels seventy afflictions from the afflictions of the world, including the evil death. Its performer will never die an evil death, along with whatever is stored up for its performer in the Hereafter.

key_terms.الصَّدَقَة: Sadaqa — voluntary charity, broader than zakat; includes any act of giving for God's sake
key_terms.بَلِيَّة: Bala/Baliyya — affliction, trial, calamity, divine test
key_terms.مِيتَة السَّوْء: Mitat al-saw' — evil death; dying in a state of sin, sudden death without repentance, or a dishonourable end
key_terms.يُدَّخَر: Yuddakhar — to be stored/reserved; the divine promise of accumulated reward awaiting the giver

ai.seo_question: What are the benefits of giving charity (sadaqa) according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) declares that giving charity (sadaqa) protects the believer from seventy worldly afflictions and from dying an evil death, while also accruing immense rewards in the Hereafter. This teaching was addressed to early Shia Muslims who lived under difficult conditions in Umayyad-era Iraq, encouraging them to practice generosity even in hardship. The number 'seventy' is a classical Arabic idiom for a large, comprehensive number rather than a strict literal count, and 'evil death' (mitat al-saw') refers to dying in a state of sin, disgrace, or sudden calamity.
